The announcement came from CVS Health.

The recognition adds a technology angle to a broader strategic reset. On November 4, CVS Health announced plans to separate into two publicly traded companies in the first half of 2028, subject to customary conditions and regulatory steps. The proposed healthcare solutions company would include Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health, while CVS Pharmacy would comprise the retail pharmacy and community healthcare operations. Existing shareholders are expected to own shares in both companies after completion, according to the company announcement.

CVS Health also reported third-quarter results on November 4. Revenue reached 108.4 billion US dollars, while adjusted earnings per share rose to 2.09 US dollars from 1.60 US dollars in the year-earlier quarter. The company raised its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings-per-share guidance to at least 8.20 US dollars and operating cash-flow guidance to at least 15.5 billion US dollars. Management nevertheless cited elevated cost trends and possible macroeconomic headwinds in its outlook. The third-quarter release said the improvement reflected stronger adjusted operating income, particularly in Health Care Benefits.

On November 4, 2026, CVS Health (NYSE:CVS | CVS Price Prediction) reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $2.09 against a $1.6508 consensus, a 26.61% surprise. The split is a stated purpose. The filing record for November 4 shows a press release, not a Form 8-K. On the call, management said the remaining company, CVS Health, would keep Aetna, Caremark, Specialty Pharmacy, Oak Street and Signify Health. CEO David Joyner said on the call, “We take this action from a position of strength.”

CVS: Shareholders are expected to own shares in both companies. Most of the value remains with the insurer and PBM (pharmacy benefit manager). In the third quarter, Health Services brought in $53,964,000,000 of revenue, against $35,498,000,000 for Pharmacy & Consumer Wellness, which shrank 2.0%.

sum: Cardinal Health reported a strong start to fiscal 2027 on November 5, with first-quarter revenue rising 5 percent year over year to 67.5 billion US dollars. The healthcare distributor also raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook, according to the company's November 5 press release.

GAAP operating earnings increased 13 percent to 753 million US dollars, while GAAP diluted earnings per share rose 27 percent to 2.38 US dollars. On a non-GAAP basis, operating earnings increased 17 percent to 1.0 billion US dollars and adjusted diluted EPS climbed 28 percent to 3.26 US dollars.

The Pharmaceutical and Specialty Solutions segment remained the main earnings driver. Revenue grew 6 percent to 62.6 billion US dollars and segment profit increased 17 percent to 783 million US dollars, supported by brand and specialty pharmaceutical sales and a favorable contribution from the generics program.

Performance was more mixed in Global Medical Products and Distribution. Revenue was broadly flat at 3.2 billion US dollars, while segment profit fell 28 percent to 33 million US dollars because of unfavorable distribution and foreign-exchange effects. Cardinal Health's Other businesses delivered stronger momentum, with revenue up 7 percent to 1.8 billion US dollars and profit up 16 percent to 193 million US dollars.

Cardinal Health lifted its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP diluted EPS range to 12.80 to 13.00 US dollars from 12.40 to 12.60 US dollars previously. The new range implies growth of 17 to 19 percent against the fiscal 2026 baseline excluding the tariff refund, and 14 to 15 percent against reported fiscal 2026 results.

Management also raised its Pharmaceutical and Specialty Solutions profit-growth outlook to 10 to 12 percent from 8 to 11 percent. The expected growth range for Other profit increased to 17 to 20 percent from 15 to 18 percent, while Other revenue growth is now expected at 12 to 14 percent. The company lowered its expected non-GAAP effective tax rate to 18.5 to 19.5 percent from 19.0 to 20.0 percent.

Hims & Hers Health (HIMS) stock rose 8.1% on Friday, November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 gained 0.3%. The advance came the same day Hims & Hers and Eli Lilly announced an agreement covering two of Lilly’s obesity drugs, Zepbound and Foundayo. What does the agreement change for Hims & Hers customers, and why does weight loss matter to the company?

Under the agreement, eligible patients who get a prescription from a licensed provider on the Hims & Hers platform can buy Zepbound and Foundayo at the same self-pay prices open to any patient, without leaving the platform. Hims & Hers already works with another drug maker, Novo Nordisk. Management said on its August 10, 2026 call that it was thrilled with the strength of that relationship.

Weight loss already shows up in the results. Q2 FY2026 revenue was $753 million, up 38.2% from a year earlier. Management said on the same call that a large part of that quarter’s beat came from the weight category being much stronger than it had thought. Yet management expects gross margins to stay below past levels as branded weight loss products and international revenue grow. The reported gross margin was 63.8% in Q2 FY2026, against 76% a year earlier.
Hims & Hers moved on its own. The SPDR health care sector fund, XLV, slipped 0.1% during the same session, a day the S&P 500 barely moved. Among its peers, CVS Health rose 3.1% and Cigna fell 2.6%.

A rise this large is not rare for this stock: Hims & Hers had 17 sessions with a gain at least this big in the prior 365 days. Friday’s gain also came one session after a 9.8% fall on Thursday, November 5.

Over the past year, the stock fell 40.5%, against a 9.8% gain for the S&P 500. Its $26.00 close is still well above its 52-week closing low of $14.52, set on February 27, 2026. CVS Announces Split Into Two: Pharmacy and Insurance to Separate, Shares Plunge More Than 12% in a Single Day
sum: U.S. healthcare giant CVS Health (CVS) announced a major organizational restructuring on Wednesday (November 4), planning to split the group into two independent publicly traded companies, one focused on retail pharmacy and the other on insurance and medical services. The news was not met with market applause, as CVS shares plunged about 12.5% that day, reflecting investor concerns over the lack of detail on the separation.

Under the plan, the company retaining the CVS Health name will continue to be led by current Chief Executive Officer David Joyner, with operations spanning Aetna health insurance, CVS Caremark pharmacy benefit management (PBM), the CVS Specialty business, and medical services businesses including Oak Street Health and Signify Health. The other independent company will be named CVS Pharmacy, with current group President Prem Shah serving as CEO, encompassing roughly 9,000 physical pharmacies, mail-order pharmacy, MinuteClinic retail clinics, and the Health100 technology services platform.

The separation is expected to be completed in the first half of 2028 and remains subject to regulatory approvals. CVS emphasized that existing customers' prescription drugs, medical services and insurance benefits will not be immediately affected; upon completion of the separation, existing shareholders will hold shares in both companies, and the transaction is structured to be tax-free.

Explaining the decision, Joyner said that over the past two years, operations at the company's 9,000 pharmacies, Caremark and Aetna had all improved markedly, which gave the company the conditions to undertake the organizational restructuring. He noted that the pharmacy side boosted throughput by upgrading store technology and adjusted its prescription reimbursement model so that it can offer lower prices while still maintaining margins on branded and generic drugs. He also said bluntly in an interview: "Every business is executing very well, and we now have the room to make different decisions that I couldn't have made two years ago."
Paradoxically, the third-quarter results CVS reported the same day were not bad at all.

CVS Settles DOJ Opioid Case for $315 Million: Here’s What It Means for the Stock
sum: CVS Health (CVS) agreed on Tuesday, October 13, to pay $315 million to settle a Justice Department lawsuit over opioid prescriptions, Reuters reported. The government alleged that CVS pharmacies filled invalid prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances from October 2013 through December 2025, then billed Medicare and other federal programs for many of them. CVS didn’t admit wrongdoing and says it disagrees with the claims.
The stock barely noticed. CVS closed at $87.55 on Tuesday, down 0.2%, and was flat before Wednesday’s open.
- $315 million to resolve claims under the Controlled Substances Act and the False Claims Act
- A hotline for employees and the public to report suspicious prescriptions, plus monitoring of dispensing patterns (AP)
- No admission of liability (the case began as a former employee’s whistleblower suit, and the government filed its own complaint in December 2024)

CVS generated $10.64 billion of cash from operations in 2025 and has guided to at least $11.5 billion this year. The settlement is under 3% of either figure, or about 25 cents a share against an $88 stock.

It’s also the second federal case CVS has closed since July. CVS and Omnicare, its long-term care pharmacy unit, agreed to settle for at least $440 million against a judgment of nearly $950 million. CVS pays $130 million within two weeks of the agreement taking effect and covers any shortfall in a further $310 million if Omnicare’s estate hasn’t paid it by March 2028. Together, the two settlements come to about $755 million, roughly 7% of last year’s operating cash flow. Walmart (WMT) settled its own DOJ opioid-dispensing case for $50 million in August.

items.t: CVS Health (CVS) Upgraded to Buy: What Does It Mean for the Stock?
sum: Investors might want to bet on CVS Health (CVS), as it has been recently upgraded to a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). An upward trend in earnings estimates -- one of the most powerful forces impacting stock prices -- has triggered this rating change.

The sole determinant of the Zacks rating is a company's changing earnings picture. The Zacks Consensus Estimate -- the consensus of EPS estimates from the sell-side analysts covering the stock -- for the current and following years is tracked by the system.

Since a changing earnings picture is a powerful factor influencing near-term stock price movements, the Zacks rating system is very useful for individual investors. They may find it difficult to make decisions based on rating upgrades by Wall Street analysts, as these are mostly driven by subjective factors that are hard to see and measure in real time.
Therefore, the Zacks rating upgrade for CVS Health basically reflects positivity about its earnings outlook that could translate into buying pressure and an increase in its stock price.

The change in a company's future earnings potential, as reflected in earnings estimate revisions, has proven to be strongly correlated with the near-term price movement of its stock. The influence of institutional investors has a partial contribution to this relationship, as these big professionals use earnings and earnings estimates to calculate the fair value of a company's shares. An increase or decrease in earnings estimates in their valuation models simply results in higher or lower fair value for a stock, and institutional investors typically buy or sell it. Their bulk investment action then leads to price movement for the stock.

For CVS Health, rising earnings estimates and the consequent rating upgrade fundamentally mean an improvement in the company's underlying business. And investors' appreciation of this improving business trend should push the stock higher.

Empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock movements, so it could be truly rewarding if such revisions are tracked for making an investment decision. Here is where the tried-and-tested Zacks Rank stock-rating system plays an important role, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions.

CVS agrees to pay $38M to resolve insulin over-distribution allegations, DOJ says
sum: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced Tuesday that it reached a settlement with CVS Health after authorities accused the healthcare giant of over-dispensing insulin pens to patients and billing Medicare, Medicaid and other government programs for the cost.

The case, now resolved for nearly $37.8 million, was brought by a whistleblower under protections of the False Claims Act. In this case, that’s Adam Rahimi, a former CVS pharmacist who will receive 19.5% of that amount, split between him and his attorneys—though the latter said their client will receive "most of those proceeds."

As is common, the DOJ joined the case after it found Rahimi’s accusations to be credible. According to the agency, between January 10, 2010 and December 31, 2020, CVS pharmacists handed out more insulin pens than were prescribed by clinicians, then billing the government for unnecessary “refills” that a patient didn’t need.

To cover its tracks, CVS would allegedly underreport its insulin supplies so records would match. The company allegedly told its pharmacists to lie about the “days-of-supply” its pharmacies had of insulin—meaning the expected number of days its supplies were expected to last—in order to justify the claims submitted to Medicare and Medicaid.

“CVS management was well aware that it was over-dispensing insulin,” the DOJ wrote in its complaint. “Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) conducted periodic audits of CVS pharmacies and repeatedly found violations of the dispensing rules, including reporting invalid days-of-supply data, refilling insulin pen prescriptions too soon, and dispensing insulin pens in excess of the quantities authorized by the prescription.”

The agency went on to claim that the PBMs “issued chargebacks to CVS based on these violations” but that the pharmacies never took the “necessary steps to address this long-standing problem” of misreported insulin stocks and over-distribution.

These issues occurred in multiple states, with safety net programs often billed for the insulin. While states will receive some money from this settlement, the DOJ said the bulk of it—$24.5 million—will go to the federal government.

sum: One of the hottest healthcare stocks to own this year has undoubtedly been CVS Health (CVS -1.59%). It's up 75% while the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund has climbed by just 6%. The performance, does, however, warrant an asterisk as CVS is coming off a brutal year in 2024 when it crashed more than 43%. The stock was beaten down and may have appealed to value-oriented investors.

Nonetheless, the company must be doing something right for investors to be significantly more bullish on the stock this year; a low valuation on its own usually isn't enough to give the stock this type of a boost. And even though the stock has rallied so much this year, CVS still doesn't look all that expensive given its level of profitability.

A year ago, the situation for CVS didn't look all that great. The company's results were underwhelming as it continually missed expectations due to high costs in its insurance business. Ultimately, it withdrew its guidance for the year and made a change in CEO, with David Joyner coming on and replacing Karen Lynch.

The company's growth rate, which was falling last year, has been steadily improving in recent quarters. However, that's also going to be easier to do when going up against weaker comparables from the previous year, so investors should consider the context.

But at the very least, the business isn't continually disappointing investors and Wall Street as a whole. Its latest numbers, for the third quarter (which ended on Sept. 30), came in better than anticipated. CVS's adjusted earnings per share of $1.60 were easily above analyst expectations of $1.37. Meanwhile, revenue of $102.9 billion was up 8% and also better than the $98.9 billion that Wall Street was looking for.
With more stability in its business these days and improvements showing in its bottom line, investors have become more bullish on the healthcare stock recently, and rightfully so.

When a stock experiences a significant surge in value, oftentimes it means its valuation has become bloated, and it may not be worth investing in the business anymore. But that's not the case with CVS. Although the stock is up big this year, when you consider its level of earnings, it's still not an expensive investment to hold in your portfolio.
